abstract: In real life, success is often contingent upon multiple critical steps that are distant in time from each other and from the final reward. These critical steps are challenging to identify with traditional reinforcement learning (RL) methods that rely on the Bellman equation for credit assignment. Here, we present a new RL algorithm that uses offline contrastive learning to hone in on these critical steps. This algorithm, which we call Contrastive Retrospection (ConSpec), can be added to any existing RL algorithm. ConSpec learns a set of prototypes for the critical steps in a task by a novel contrastive loss and delivers an intrinsic reward when the current state matches one of the prototypes. The prototypes in ConSpec provide two key benefits for credit assignment: (i) They enable rapid identification of all the critical steps. (ii) They do so in a readily interpretable manner, enabling out-of-distribution generalization when sensory features are altered. Distinct from other contemporary RL approaches to credit assignment, ConSpec takes advantage of the fact that it is easier to retrospectively identify the small set of steps that success is contingent upon (and ignoring other states) than it is to prospectively predict reward at every taken step. ConSpec greatly improves learning in a diverse set of RL tasks. The code is available at the link: https://github.com/sunchipsster1/ConSpec

# CONTRASTIVE INTROSPECTION TO IDENTIFY CRITICAL STEPS IN REINFORCEMENT LEARNING

Chen Sun*

Mila, Université de Montréal

# ABSTRACT

In real life, success is often contingent upon multiple critical steps that are distant in time from each other and from the final reward. These critical steps can be challenging to identify with traditional reinforcement learning (RL) methods that rely on the Bellman equation for credit assignment. Here, we present a new RL algorithm that uses offline contrastive learning to identify critical steps in any task. This algorithm, which we call contrastive introspection (ConSpec), can be added to any existing RL algorithm. ConSpec learns a set of prototypes for the critical steps in a task and delivers an intrinsic reward when the current state matches one of these prototypes. The prototypes in ConSpec provide two key benefits for credit assignment: (1) They enable rapid identification of all the critical steps. (2) They do so in a readily interpretable manner, enabling out-of-distribution generalization when sensory features are altered. We show that ConSpec improves learning in both tasks with explicit critical steps (e.g. when a key must be collected to open a door) and tasks with no immediately obvious critical steps (e.g. continuous control tasks). In summary, ConSpec is a modular component that can be added to any existing RL algorithm to improve performance.

# 1 INTRODUCTION

In real life, success in any given task often involves multiple critical steps. For example, consider the steps necessary for getting a paper accepted at an AI conference. One must generate a good idea, conduct mathematical analyses or experiments that successfully validate the idea, create figures, write a paper, submit the paper, and finally, respond to reviewer comments in a satisfactory manner. Skipping any of these steps will lead to failure.

Though such situations are common in real life, they are highly nontrivial for most RL algorithms. The problem is that the traditional approach for credit assignment in RL, using the Bellman equation (Sutton & Barto, 2018; Bellman, 1957), will take a lot of time to propagate value estimates back to the earlier critical steps if the length of time between critical steps is sufficiently long (Raposo et al., 2021; Puigdomenech Badia et al., 2020). The classic solution to this problem is to try to identify "bottleneck states", i.e. states that must be visited to obtain reward, then use the bottleneck states as sub-goals (McGovern &

Barto, 2001; Nachum et al., 2018; Sasha Vezhnevets et al., 2017; Sutton et al., 1999; Bacon et al., 2016). The problem with this approach is that the critical steps in non-toy tasks rarely correspond to specific states of the environment. Instead, there are "many ways to skin a cat", meaning that there can be a large, potentially even infinite, set of states that correspond to taking a critical step in a task. For example, what are the "states" associated with "conducting a mathematical analysis" for AI research? Ultimately, we need AI systems that can learn how to identify critical steps without assuming that they correspond to any specific state or easily identifiable set of states.

Some recent work has attempted to address this problem using memory. In these approaches, the system attempts to predict value or reward using both the current state and the past states in the memory buffer selected by attention or other means (Arjona-Medina et al., 2018; Hung et al., 2019; Raposo et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2021; Parisotto et al., 2019; Goyal et al., 2019; 2020). In doing so, these approaches can avoid the slow process of using the Bellman equation for propagating value. However, they are still not capable of identifying critical steps for success, especially when a successful critical step can be achieved by myriad actual states (e.g., all the "good ideas", all the ways to write a good paper on the idea, etc).

Here, we present an algorithm designed to identify critical steps of a task in a scalable manner. Our approach, which we call contrastive introspection (ConSpec), uses offline learning from a memory buffer with a contrastive loss that identifies invariances amongst successful episodes, i.e., the family of states corresponding to a successfully achieved critical step. This family of states is associated with a learned feature via a function mapping the input observations to a score that is large when the critical step is achieved. To do this, ConSpec learns a state encoder and a series of prototypes<sup>1</sup> that represent critical steps. The score is large when the representation of the input state at the output of the encoder is well aligned with a prototype for the critical step. ConSpec then delivers intrinsic rewards (Schmidhuber, 2010; Randlov & Alstrom, 1998) to the RL agent whenever it detects a match to its prototypes, thereby steering the policy towards achieving the corresponding critical steps. Other works that harness contrastive learning in RL have not utilized it for the purpose of discovering critical steps. Instead, they either apply contrastive learning directly as a regularizer for representation learning (Srinivas et al., 2020), or they use it to learn whole policies (Anand et al., 2019; Sermanet et al., 2017; Finn et al., 2016; Ghosh et al., 2019; Eysenbach et al., 2022; Li et al., 2021; Agarwal et al., 2021). We show that the addition of ConSpec to an RL agent greatly improves long-term credit assignment, both for tasks with explicit critical steps (such as a task where a key must be found to open a door) and tasks with no obvious critical steps (such as continuous control tasks like the half-cheetah). As well, we demonstrate that the invariant nature of the learned prototypes for the critical steps also helps with few-shot out-of-distribution generalization. Thus, ConSpec is a promising approach to improving RL in a wide variety of applications. It moreover has the added benefit that the learned prototypes are readily interpretable and could be used for other downstream purposes.

# 2 CONTRASTIVE INTROSPECTION FOR IDENTIFYING CRITICAL STEPS

Humans are very good at recognizing when their success is contingent upon multiple past steps. Moreover, they are very fast at recognizing these contingencies—even children can identify contingencies in a task after only a handful of experiences (Sobel et al., 2004; Gopnik & Sobel, 2000). Intuitively, humans achieve this by engaging in introspection to examine their past and determine which steps along the way were necessary for success. Such introspection often seems to involve a comparison: we seem to be good at identifying the differences between the situations that led to success and those that led to failure, and then we hone in on these differences. We reasoned that it would be possible for AI systems to learn to identify critical steps—and moreover, do so robustly—if a system were equipped with a similar capability to take advantage of memory to sort through the events that distinguished successful versus failed episodes. This paper's principal contribution is the introduction of an add-on architecture and loss for introspection of this sort: contrastive introspection (ConSpec) (Fig. 1).

![](images/e9b9087bd8d72f08daa17a0b70d15cb9080139d0c4bd262fac7a109dbf21c60c.jpg)  
Figure 1: ConSpec is a module that can help any backbone RL system. ConSpec trains its prototypes by comparing successful v. failed episodes via a contrastive loss, and uses the match to these prototypes to output intrinsic rewards to the RL agent.

At its core, ConSpec is a mechanism by which a contrastive loss enables rapid learning of a set of prototypes for recognizing critical steps. Below we describe how ConSpec works.

# 2.1 A SET OF INVARIANT PROTOTYPES FOR CRITICAL STEPS

To recognize when a new observation corresponds to a critical step, we store a set of  $H$  prototypes in a learned representation space. Each prototype,  $h_i$  is a learned vector that is compared to a non-linear projection of the latent representation of currently encoded features in the environment,  $g_{\theta}(z_t)$  (with projection parameters  $\theta$ ). Thus, if we have current observation  $O_t$ , encoded as a latent state  $z_t = f_W(O_t)$  (with encoder parameters  $W$ ), we compare  $g_{\theta}(z_t)$  to each of the prototypes,  $h_i$ , in order to assess whether the current observation corresponds to a critical step or not. Using cosine similarity, which involves a dot product  $h_i \cdot z_t$  between the prototype  $h_i$  and the encoder output  $z_t$ , can detect a large class of states because the mapping from  $O_t$  to  $h_i \cdot f_W(O_t)$  is a many-to-one mapping, similar to a neural net classifier.

At first glance, one might think that the number of prototypes would have to be very large, since there are a massive number of potential states in non-toy tasks. However, this is not actually the case because we learn the encoder  $f_{W}$ . ConSpec is designed to discover prototypes and an encoder that captures invariant features across successful episodes (see next section on the contrastive loss function for achieving this invariance). Therefore, there can be an infinite number of states that match any given prototype, and so, the number of prototypes can actually be quite small. In what follows, we used  $H \leq 20$  for all our tasks, even the ones in 3D environments and with continuous control which have a lot of state-level variation. Of course, in other settings more prototypes may need to be used, and the number required would have to be empirically determined.

# 2.2 A MEMORY SYSTEM FOR STORING SUCESSSES AND FAILURES

ConSpec maintains three memory buffers: one for the current mini-batch being trained on  $(\mathcal{B}$ ; with a capacity of  $M_{\mathcal{B}}$ ), one for successful episodes  $(S$ ; with a capacity of  $M_S$ ), and one for failure episodes  $(\mathcal{F}$ ; with a capacity of  $M_{\mathcal{F}}$ ). Each episode is of length  $T$  time steps. As we show, these memory buffers need not be very large for ConSpec to work; we find that 16 slots in memory is enough, even for 3D environments. As well, it should be noted that this system requires a definition of "success" in any task, to make the prototypes and the encoder good at discriminating success from failure. We provide our definition of success for every task presented in this paper in the Appendix A.2.

Each buffer stores raw observations,  $O_{t}$ , encountered by the agent in the environment. When a new mini-batch of observations is loaded into  $\mathcal{B}$  for training, the episodes are categorized into successes and failures using the given criteria for the task. We then fill  $S$  and  $\mathcal{F}$  with observations from those categorized episodes in a first-in-first-out (FIFO) manner, where episodes stored from previous batches are overwritten as new trajectories come in.

# 2.3 A CONTRASTIVE LOSS TO LEARN PROTOTYPES

To learn our invariant prototypes of critical steps (and the encoding of the observation) we employ a contrastive loss that differentiates successes from failures. The contrastive loss uses the observations stored in  $S$  and  $\mathcal{F}$  to shape the prototypes such that they capture invariant features shared by a spectrum of observations in successful episodes. The functional form of this loss is:

$$
\mathcal {L} _ {\mathrm {C o n S p e c}} = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {H} \frac {1}{M _ {\mathcal {S}}} \sum_ {k \in \mathcal {S}} | 1 - \max _ {t \in \{1.. T \}} s _ {i k t} | +
$$

$$
\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {H} \frac {1}{M _ {\mathcal {F}}} \sum_ {k \in \mathcal {F}} | \max  _ {t \in \{1.. T \}} s _ {i k t} | + \tag {1}
$$

$$
\alpha \cdot \frac {1}{H} \sum_ {k \in \mathcal {S}} D (\left\{\boldsymbol {s} _ {\boldsymbol {i k}} \right\} _ {1 \leq i \leq H})
$$

where  $s_{ikt} = \cos(h_i, g_\theta(z_{kt}))$  is the cosine similarity of prototype  $h_i$  and the latent representation for the observation from timestep  $t$  found in episode  $k$ ,  $s_{ik}$  is the vector of  $s_{ikt}$  elements concatenated along  $t$  and softmaxed over  $t$  to sparsify it, and  $D(\cdot)$  is a function that measures the diversity in the matches to the prototypes (see Appendix section A.4 for functions  $D(\cdot)$  we used in this work).

To elaborate on this loss, for each prototype  $h_i$  and each episode's projection at time step  $t$ ,  $g_{\theta}(z_{kt})$ , the cosine similarity (a normalized dot product) is calculated between the prototype's vector and the latent projection vectors to yield a time-series of cosine similarity scores. The maximum similarity score across time within each episode is then calculated. The maximum similarity score for each successful episode is pushed up (first term of the loss) and the maximum score for each failed episode is pushed down (second term). The 3rd term of the loss encourages the different prototypes to be distinct from one another. The ConSpec loss is added to any RL losses during off-line training (Algorithm 1 pseudocode). Below we show that this loss leads to prototypes that hone in on distinct critical steps (Fig. 4b).

# 2.4 GENERATING INTRINSIC REARDS BASED ON INTROSPECTION

Thus far, the described model learns a set of prototypes for critical steps along with an encoder. This system must still be connected to an RL agent that can learn a policy  $(\pi_{\phi},$  parameterized by  $\phi)$ . This could proceed in a number of different ways. Here, we chose the reward shaping approach (Schmidhuber, 2010; Randlov & Alstrom, 1998; Ng et al., 1999), wherein we add additional intrinsic rewards  $\tilde{r}_{kt}$  to the rewards from the environment,  $r_{kt}$  though other strategies are possible. One simple approach is to define the intrinsic reward according to the output similarity scores of prototypes for each time step. In most of the experiments presented here, we define the intrinsic reward in episode  $k$  at time-step  $t$ ,  $\tilde{r}_{kt}$  as the maximum prototype score,  $\hat{s}_{ikt}$ , across a moving window of seven time-steps (with a threshold of 0.6 applied to ignore small fluctuations in the scores). However, a concern with any reward shaping is that it can alter the underlying optimal policy (Randlov & Alstrom, 1998; Ng et al., 1999). Therefore, we experimented with another scheme for defining intrinsic rewards:

$$
\tilde {r} _ {k t} = \lambda \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {H} \left(\gamma \cdot \hat {s} _ {i k, t} - \hat {s} _ {i k, t - 1}\right) \tag {2}
$$

where  $\lambda$  is a proportionality constant and  $\gamma$  is the discount in the backbone RL algorithm. This formula for intrinsic reward can be shown to satisfy the necessary and sufficient criterion from (Ng et al., 1999) for policy invariance. Thus, if this form of the intrinsic reward is used then the ConSpec reward shaping scheme provably does not alter the optimal policy of the RL agent. In practice, we find that both forms of intrinsic reward work well. Unless otherwise noted, data shown in this paper used the first form of intrinsic reward. With the ConSpec loss and the intrinsic reward defined we then train RL agents with ConSpec added according to Algorithm 1.

# 3 EMPIRICAL RESULTS

We tested ConSpec across a variety of RL tasks: simple grid worlds, continuous control, video games, and richer 3-D environments. We demonstrate below how ConSpec is able to rapidly hone in on critical steps, and in this way, contribute to alleviating two difficult problems in RL: long term credit assignment, and out-of-distribution generalization.

# 3.1 CONSPEC LEARNS PROTOTYPES FOR CRITICAL STEPS IN 3D ENVIRONMENTS

We began with a series of experiments in a 3D virtual environment. This was to verify that ConSpec can identify critical steps in complex sensory environments, wherein critical steps do not correspond to specific observable states (as bottleneck states do). In particular, we wanted to determine whether ConSpec is able to discover invariant properties that distinguish a given critical step in a non-trivial sensory milieu. To do this, we used SilicoLabs<sup>2</sup> Unity-based (Juliani et al., 2018) game engine to create a 3-stage task that we call the "OrangeTree" task. In stage 1 of this task, the agent is placed in a room with two objects, one of them round or spiky (e.g. balls or jacks), and one of them flat (e.g. boxes or tables). The agent can pick up one of the objects (Fig. 2a), but it is not forced to. In stage 2, the agent is put in a waiting room where nothing happens. This was done to render the credit assignment problem non-trivial, since it increases the temporal separation between the first and last stage. In stage 3, the agent is placed in a new room with an orange tree. To obtain a reward, the agent must pick an orange. But to do this, it must stand on a flat object in order to reach the oranges. As such, in stage 1, if the agent had not picked up an object, or picked a spiky/round object, it would not have been able to pick an orange and obtain reward. Thus, picking up a flat object is a critical step in this task. But, because there are a variety of flat objects there is no single bottleneck state. Instead, the agent must learn that the invariant property of the critical step in the task is the flatness of the object to pick up.

ConSpecwas compared with a series of baselines. We first tested Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) (Schulman et al., 2017; Kostrikov, 2018) on this OrangeTree task. We found that PPO is not able to solve this task (Fig. 2b), because it does not learn to collect a flat object at stage 1. One possible reason for this is simply the challenge of long-term credit assignment. As such, we next tested an agent trained with PPO and Synthetic Returns (SynthRs) (Raposo et al., 2021), a recent reward shaping algorithm designed to solve long-term credit assignment problems. SynthRs works by learning to predict rewards based on past memories and delivering an intrinsic reward whenever the current state is predictive of reward. We found that adding SynthRs to the PPO agent did not help solve the problem (Fig. 2b), and the agent still failed to pick up flat objects in stage 1. This shows that the capacity to do long-term credit assignment is, by itself, not enough when success does not depend on single

bottleneck state, but rather a diverse set of states that share a critical invariant property (e.g. of flatness), and hence requires a more sophisticated credit assignment mechanism.

Thus, as an additional baseline we considered a more sophisticated technique for representation learning in RL, Contrastive Unsupervised Reinforcement Learning (CURL) (Srinivas et al., 2020), which outperforms prior pixel-based methods on complex tasks. As well, contrastive methods have been shown to be effective for learning invariant representations, thus CURL could theoretically help an agent to learn how to recognize flat objects. However, we found that like the other two baselines, adding CURL to PPO did not lead the agents to solve the OrangeTree task (Fig. 2b). This is likely because CURL is not learning invariances related to success in the task, but rather, invariances related to image perturbations.

Finally, we examined the performance of ConSpec. Specifically, we examined the performance of an agent trained with PPO, but with additional intrinsic rewards from a ConSpec module per Algorithm 1. We found that PPO with ConSpec added could indeed solve the OrangeTree task (Fig. 2b). To further dissect the reasons for ConSpec's abilities, we studied the invariances it learned, i.e. we examined the range of images that were mapped to its prototypes of critical steps. To do this, we collected successful episodes and then identified the observations (images) that maximally matched the prototypes during the episodes. Notably, one of the prototypes consistently had observations of picking up a flat object mapped to it. In other words, this prototype had discovered an invariant feature of a critical step that was common to all successes but not failures, namely, the step of having picked up a flat object and not a spiky or round one (Fig. 2c). Moreover, this prototype learned to prefer flat objects regardless of the type of object (i.e. box or table) and regardless of its colour. As such, the contrastive learning of ConSpec permitted the prototype to learn to recognize a critical step, namely picking up flat objects, and to maintain invariance to irrelevant features of those objects, such as shape and colour.

# 3.2 CONSPEC GENERALIZES TO NEW CONTINGENCIES IN 3D ENVIRONMENTS

We next asked whether ConSpec's capacity for finding invariances among critical steps could aid in zero-shot generalization when the sensory features of the environment were altered. To test this, we made a variation of the OrangeTree task. During training, the agent saw flat objects that were magenta, blue, red, green, yellow, or peach (Fig. 3a). During testing, a black table or box was presented, even though the agent had never seen black objects before. Intuitively, for the agent to succeed in this situation it must immediately recognize the black table or box as a flat object that is critical for success despite its total lack of experience with black objects. Indeed, investigation of the images matched to the prototypes showed that the prototype that recognized picking up flat objects immediately generalized to black flat objects (Fig. 3b). Thanks to this, the agent with PPO and ConSpec successfully solved the task with the black objects with no more training, i.e. in a zero-shot manner (Fig. 3e). This shows that ConSpec was able to learn prototypes that discovered an invariant feature among successes (flatness), and was not confused by irrelevant sensory features such as colour, permitting it to generalize to contingencies involving colours never seen before.

To further test ConSpec's capacity for generalization, we made another variation of the OrangeTree task with the background environment changed, in a manner typical of out-of-distribution (OoD) generalization tests (Arjovsky, 2021). In particular, testing took place in a different room than training, such that the new room had pink walls and a green floor (unlike the gray walls and blue floor of the training room) (Fig. 3c). Again, the prototypes generalized in a zero-shot manner, with flat objects being mapped to the appropriate prototype in the new environment despite the different background 3d). However, the policy was slightly affected by the change in environment, leading to a small drop in the median reward obtained. But, after a brief period of acclimatization to the new environment (where the underlying PPO agent was trained for no more than 20 gradient descent steps while ConSpec was kept constant), the ConSpec agent was able to rapidly solve the task (Fig. 3f). For comparison, training from scratch in OrangeTree takes PPO with ConSpec hundreds of steps, and vanilla PPO by itself cannot train on the task at all within the allotted time. Moreover, as noted, the prototypes themselves were not trained further in the new environment. Thus, the learned prototypes ability to zero-shot generalize allowed the agents to rapidly retrain their policies. Altogether, ConSpec's contrastive learning of prototypes allow an agent not only to rapidly hone in on critical steps, but also, ConSpec's prototypes have the added perk that the ability to recognize a critical step seems robust enough to help the agent rapidly generalize to new but related environments.

# 3.3 CONSPEC DOES BETTER LONG TERM CREDIT ASSIGNMENT IN GRID WORLD TASKS WITH MULTIPLE CRITICAL STEPS

ConSpec's contrastive system for learning prototypes of critical steps appears to simultaneously confer two major benefits to RL systems. First, the prototypes hone in on critical steps, then provide intrinsic rewards for them, thereby mitigating the challenge of long-term credit assignment. Second, the learned prototypes reflect robust, invariant features, helping out-of-distribution generalization, as we showed above.

To further investigate ConSpec's ability to engage in long-term credit assignment by identifying critical steps, we used simple multi-key-to-door tasks in a 2D grid world environment. The shift to 2D from 3D allowed us to run many more simulations, and longer simulations, which enabled us to test situations where there are multiple critical steps separated by long periods of time. In the multi-key-to-door tasks we used here, the agent must find one or more keys to open one or more doors (Fig. 4a). If the agent does not pick up all of the keys and does not pass through all of the doors, success is impossible. To make the tasks more

challenging for traditional Bellman back-ups, the agent is forced to wait in a waiting room for many time steps in-between the retrieval of each key. An episode is successful if and only if the agent exits the final door.

An important difference with other contemporary approaches to tackle the long-term credit assignment problem is that whereas other solutions have a search space that scales with the number of critical steps that success is contingent upon, ConSpec has a constant search space. In fact, a key motivation for our design of ConSpec is that learning a full model of the world and its transitions and values may be very difficult, especially for a novice agent (Arjona-Medina et al., 2018; Hung et al., 2019; Raposo et al., 2021; Ren et al., 2021). As well, predicting success as a function of previous steps can be a highly nontrivial non-linear function. By contrast, ConSpec avoids learning a full model of the world and simply focuses on identifying critical steps, a much more limited task that can be done rapidly. As such, we would expect a clear difference to emerge between ConSpec and other solutions that rely on predicting reward as we increase the number of critical steps required for success. The multi-key-to-door tasks allowed us to test this hypothesis.

We found that when ConSpec was trained in these tasks, each prototype learned to represent a distinct critical key-retrieval step (e.g. one prototype learned to hone in on the retrieval of the first key, another prototype on the second key, etc.). We demonstrated this by examining which state in different episodes maximally matched each prototype. As can be seen, picking up the first key was matched to one prototype, picking up the second was matched to another, and so on (Fig. 4b). Thus, ConSpec identifies multiple critical steps in a highly interpretable manner in the multi-key-to-door tasks.

We then tested ConSpec atop a PPO backbone again. We compared performance to two other baseline solutions to long-term credit assignment in RL. The first baseline was SynthRs. The second baseline was a Temporal Value Transport (TVT) system (Hung et al., 2019). TVT uses a Reconstructive Memory Agent (RMA) (Hung et al., 2019; Wayne et al., 2018) that allows it to "transport" Bellman updates far back into the history of the agent in order to overcome long-term credit assignment challenges.

We found that PPO with ConSpec learns the multi-key-to-door tasks very rapidly, across a range of number of keys (Fig. 4c, left). Importantly, even as keys got added, ConSpec's training time remained constant when the exploration required for new keys was accounted for (Fig. 4c, right). On the other hand, though Synths and TVT solve the task for a single key thanks to their ability to do long-term credit assignment (Fig. 9), their performance collapsed as more keys get added (Fig. 4d). This highlights the difficulty of long-term credit assignment when there are multiple critical steps. Hence, though learning when there are multiple critical steps separated by long periods of time is difficult, it is easily accommodated by ConSpec. We discuss this in more depth in the Appendix section A.5.

Finally, we note that ConSpec learned these tasks not only atop a PPO backbone, but also atop an RMA backbone (Fig. 10 and also Fig. 9b), illustrating ConSpec's flexibility. This suggests that ConSpec can be added to any RL system to discover critical steps and improve long-term credit assignment.

# 3.4 CONSPEC HELPS CREDIT ASSIGNMENT IN NON-TOY VIDEO GAME TASKS, INCLUDING MONTEZUMA'S REVENGE

Next we studied whether ConSpec can help credit assignment in other tasks not specifically designed to contain multiple critical steps. That is not to say that other RL tasks do not contain critical steps, rather, that they are not designed to highlight them. We began by testing on a suite of Atari games from the OpenAI Gym (Brockman et al., 2016).

First, we note that ConSpec, like other algorithms that generate intrinsic rewards for reward shaping, must do so carefully because reward shaping can alter the optimal policy. As noted in the 2.4 section, one way to deal with this problem is to take advantage of a formal proof from Ng. et al (Ng et al., 1999), which provides the necessary and sufficient condition for a reward shaping function to leave the optimal policy unperturbed. We implemented a version of ConSpec that respects this condition (equation 2) and tested it on a suite of Atari games.

We first note that existing RL algorithms, such as PPO, are sufficient to solve many, but not all, of these games. Crucially, we found that across the eight Atari games we tested performance was not hurt by adding ConSpec to PPO, in-line with the formal proof that this form of reward shaping would not alter the optimal policy (Fig. 5).

As well, even when we used our first formulation of the intrinsic reward (see 2.4), ConSpec did not hurt performance on the Atari games. We speculate that even with this simple formulation of the intrinsic reward ConSpec does not drastically alter the optimal policy because it confers intrinsic rewards very sparingly and according to a relatively stringent criterion. Thus, the data provided here suggest that ConSpec can be safely added to existing RL systems without negative consequences.

Of course, although PPO alone solves many of the Atari games, it does not solve all of them. Most notably, it does not solve Montezuma's Revenge, and its performance does not usually exceed 0 reward. Montezuma's Revenge's difficulty is usually considered to be an exploration challenge. But interestingly, we see that ConSpec improves performance on Montezuma's Revenge even without any sophisticated exploration techniques added (Fig. 6a). To provide intuition as to why ConSpec is able to help even in the absence of dedicated exploration algorithms, we studied how many successful trajectories it takes for ConSpec to learn how to obtain at least the first reward in the game. Crucially, ConSpec atop PPO with only a simple  $\epsilon$ -greedy exploration system is able to learn the game with as few as 2 successful episodes (Fig. 6b). We speculate that this is because ConSpec, like other contrastive techniques (Chen et al., 2020), benefits mostly from a large number of negative samples (i.e. failures) which are easy to obtain. This also fits the real-life intuition that all that should be required to recognize critical steps is one or two successful demonstrations, from which useful knowledge can be extracted. Hence, altogether, ConSpec uses successes very efficiently, allowing it to solve challenging tasks like Montezuma's Revenge.

# 3.5 CONSPEC HELPS CREDIT ASSIGNMENT IN CONTINUOUS CONTROL TASKS

Finally, we studied whether ConSpec might help even in tasks that do not explicitly involve discrete steps, such as continuous control tasks. These tasks are interesting because both the robotics and neurophysiology literature has long known that atomic "moves" can be extracted from the structure of continuous control policies (d'Avella & Bizzi, 2005; Thomas & Barto, 2012). Moreover, this is evident in real life, where even though learning to play the piano or running are continuous control tasks, oftentimes we can still identify specific critical steps that are required (such as playing arpeggios smoothly or when your foot makes contact with the floor). However, contemporary RL algorithms for continual control tasks are not designed to hone in on these sparse critical steps, and instead, they focus on learning the Markovian state-to-state policy.

We focused on three continuous control tasks: Half Cheetah, Walker, and Hopper. Each of these tasks are solvable by vanilla PPO, so we made them more challenging by delaying the reward (see Appendix section A.3). We found that ConSpec atop PPO is able to significantly improve performance in all three delayed continuous control tasks (Fig. 7b), showing the utility of learning to identify critical steps even in continuous control tasks.

# 4 DISCUSSION AND RELATED WORK

In this paper we presented ConSpec, a contrastive learning system that can be added to any RL agent to help it to identify critical steps for success from sparse rewards. We showed that this helps with both long-term credit assignment and generalization. ConSpec works by learning prototypes of critical steps with a contrastive loss that differentiates successful

![](images/a74729dec692733736160b58ba2473aaaa0ee420562a3b89d559d02208b7f12f.jpg)  
Figure 7: ConSpec improves performance in delayed versions of continuous control tasks (a) Hopper, (b) Walker, (c) Half Cheetah.

episodes from failed episodes. Adding ConSpec to an RL agent allows it to solve tasks it is otherwise incapable of solving without impairing performance in other tasks. Altogether, ConSpec is a potentially powerful general add-on for RL systems.

ConSpec is a relatively simple design, but it succeeds because it centralizes several key intuitions that it shares with other important works. ConSpec shares with bottleneck states (McGovern & Barto, 2001), hierarchical RL (HRL), and options discovery (Sutton et al., 1999; Bacon et al., 2016; Nachum et al., 2018; Sasha Vezhnevets et al., 2017) the principle that learning to hone in on a sparse number of critical steps is beneficial to RL. But, unlike bottleneck state solutions, ConSpec does not assume that critical steps correspond to individual states of the environment. As well, in HRL and options discovery, how to scalably discover appropriate subgoals remains an open and unsolved problem. In contrast, ConSpec is able to identify critical steps in complex, high-dimensional tasks, such as 3D environments.

ConSpec shares inductive biases with Return Decomposition for Delayed Rewards (RUDDER) (Arjona-Medina et al., 2018), TVT (Hung et al., 2019), Synths (Raposo et al., 2021), and various attention-based architectures (Chen et al., 2021; Parisotto et al., 2019; Goyal et al., 2019; 2020) for long-term credit assignment in RL. Namely, ConSpec also assumes that the solution to long-term credit assignment involves memory. But, unlike these other contemporary solutions, ConSpec aims to directly focus on identifying critical steps, a less burdensome task than modelling the value function, reward function, or actions taken for all encountered states, as is done in these other works.

It is also worth comparing ConSpec to another promising direction for improved credit assignment in RL, namely, Decision Transformers (Chen et al., 2021). Crucially, decision transformers require expert demonstrations, and learn poorly in the absence of near-optimal behavioural demonstrations, while ConSpec does not have such a requirement (see Fig. 13 in the Appendix).

ConSpec was inspired, in part, by the contrastive learning literature in computer vision (Hadsell et al., 2006; Chen et al., 2020; van den Oord et al., 2018; He et al., 2019). Specifically, it was inspired by the principle that transforming a task into a classification problem and using well-chosen positive and negative examples can be a very powerful means of learning invariant and generalizable representations. A similar insight on the power of classification led to a recent proposal for learning affordances (Khetarpal et al., 2020), which are arguably components of the environment that are required for critical steps. As such, ConSpec shares a deep connection with this work. Along similar lines, (Srinivas et al., 2020; Anand et al., 2019; Sermanet et al., 2017; Finn et al., 2016; Ghosh et al., 2019; Eysenbach et al., 2022; Li et al., 2021; Agarwal et al., 2021) have begun to explore contrastive systems and binary classifiers to do imitation learning and RL. With these works, ConSpec shares the principle that learning an auxiliary classification task is beneficial. But these works typically use the contrastive approach to learn whole policies or value functions. In distinction to this,

ConSpec uses contrastive learning for the purpose of learning prototypes for recognizing critical steps.

# 4.1 NEUROSCIENCE INSPIRATION

Our design of ConSpec was ultimately inspired at a high level by theories from neuroscience. For example, it shares with episodic control and related algorithms (Lin, 2004; Lengyel & Dayan, 2007; Blundell et al., 2016; Pritzel et al., 2017; Moore & Atkeson, 1992; Schaul et al., 2015; Oh et al., 2018) the principle that a memory bank can be exploited for fast learning. But unlike episodic control, ConSpec exploits memory not for estimating a surrogate value function, but rather, for learning prototypes that hone in on a small number of discrete critical steps. In-line with this, ConSpec takes inspiration from the neuroscience literature on the hippocampus which suggests that the brain, too, endeavours to encode and organize episodic experience around discrete critical steps (Sun et al., 2020; Zacks et al., 2001; Zheng et al., 2022; Franklin et al., 2019). Interestingly, recent studies suggest that honing in on discrete critical states for success may in fact be key to how the brain engages in reinforcement learning altogether (Jeong et al., 2022). Contemporary RL is predicated on the Bellman equation and the idea of reward prediction. But recent evidence from dopamine circuits suggest that the brain, like ConSpec, focuses retrospectively on causes of rewards, i.e. critical steps.
